name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Enrollment-calculation trapdoor will squeeze Iowa’s public schools
text:
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds was joined by Des Moines Prep students, state legislators and other charter school advocates as she signed into law a measure making changes to charter school and homeschooling regulations May 12, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds signed Senate File 2201, the school funding bill, into law on Feb. 26. The 2% increase in per-pupil funding for the 2026-27 school year works out to $160 more per student. When the decline in public enrollment is taken into account, it’s a statewide increase of $17 million from last year’s allotment.
The law includes a massive change in calculation of enrollment formulas. Instead of a single count of certified enrollment taken Oct. 15, a second count has been added to take place on Jan. 15/the third Monday in January called “adjusted enrollment.” (Because of Martin Luther King Jr. Day, the de facto date can be as late as Jan. 18.) The average of these two numbers will become the “basic enrollment” number used for determining the following school year’s funding.
That means the tally used for calculating state supplemental aid will be an approximation in mid-November and not exact until early February. This will end up in conflict with the law requiring state aid to be set within 30 days of the governor’s budget proposal — a deadline that has repeatedly been blown. But that’s OK, since the Legislature can exempt itself from following the law.



Quotation







“The requirement of section 257.8, subsection 1, regarding the enactment of bills establishing the regular program state percent of growth within thirty days of the submission in the year preceding the base year of the governor’s budget does not apply to this division of this Act.”


– SF 2201, bottom of page 4


This change also runs closer to the deadlines schools are under to submit property tax rates (March 5) and finalize budgets (April 30). A bill that passed the House but stalled in the Senate would have limited schools to using the previous year’s allowable growth rate if state aid is not set by March 5 and enabled updates after the fact.
During debate on SF 2201, Sen. Lynn Evans, R-Aurelia, said the second enrollment count would help in situations where a student moves into a district after Oct. 15. Under the current formulas, that student’s enrollment wouldn’t get counted toward funding until two school years later.
That may sound reasonable, but the overwhelming majority of Iowa districts are losing enrollment, and this only applies to changes in the student body over a three-month period.
The trapdoor with this second count was sprung in a different bill, House File 2754, which mainly concerns charter schools. Rep. Skyler Wheeler, R-Hull, said in opening remarks on the House floor April 16: “This is our One Big Beautiful School Choice Bill, or the one-double-B-S-C-B as we like to call it. This bill is big, and it is beautiful.”
HF 2754 includes a section allowing applications for a student to leave a public school at semester break and take half the value of that year’s state cost per pupil with them as education savings account money. An e-mail from IDOE’s Heather Doe said data updated with the second count “will include certified enrollment counts for public districts and the second ESA student enrollment period.” The exact dollar amount in ESAs overall will depend on it.
On April 27, the same evening that the Senate sent HF 2754 to the governor, the Cedar Rapids Community School District voted to close six schools and reconfigure its entire grade lineup starting in 2027. (Reynolds signed the bill May 12, during National Charter Schools Week, while surrounded by charter school students and advocates.) Another division of HF 2754 puts teacher salary supplement funding in the bundle of money that goes with each student from a public school to a charter school. Based on information from the Legislative Services Agency, that would have cost the Cedar Rapids district an additional $270,000 this past year.
“The continual attacks, generally speaking, against the ESA program I find to be fascinating,” Wheeler said on April 16. “I find it to be fascinating entirely because it has been effective. Parents have been empowered. And so we’re going to get upset, generally speaking, because parents were given the ability to go a different route. There hasn’t been a mass exodus.”
Public school enrollment in Iowa for 2025-26 had the most substantial yearly decreases, in both number and percent, in four decades, while private school enrollment increased 26% in three years to a level not seen in a quarter-century. If that’s not a “mass exodus,” what is?
Who’s not complaining?


Last winter, the Senate wanted a 1.75% increase in state aid, the House wanted 2.25%, and the compromise was 2%. The difference in the one-half percent was $18.9 million statewide, or only $2.1 million more than was spent on ESAs for students in the Davenport school district alone in the 2025-26 school year.


“You know who’s not complaining about a 1.75% increase?” Sen. Jesse Green, R-Harcourt, asked Feb. 10 during floor debate on the original version of SF 2201. “Those private schools. They’re working with a heck of a lot less, and they are happy.”
In 2022, the year before ESAs, Dowling Catholic High School’s tuition was $9,132 for parish families and $12,776 for non-parish families. In 2025, it was $11,076 plus $364 in fees for parish families and $15,498 plus fees for nonparish families. Dowling is also engaged in a $76 million capital campaign that did not require 60% supermajority approval from any public electorate.
Holy Family Catholic Schools in Dubuque raised its tuition from $2,200 in 2022 to $11,500 in 2025.
Siouxland Christian’s tuition went up 18% from 2024 to 2025.
Hull Christian School, which last year received more than $1.25 million in ESA money from students living in the Boyden-Hull school district, broke ground March 27 on a $4.7 million expansion.
Iowa does not require private schools to publish budgets or curriculum information. Iowa does not require them to have public meetings before major construction.
Private schools wouldn’t even have been bound by a bill of Wheeler’s that was approved by the House Education Committee on Feb. 11, but died later in the session, mandating that all students at public schools conform to a statewide dress code.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Conservative legal organization sues – again — over constitutionality of DFL’s 2024 omnibus
text:
House Minority Leader Lisa Demuth and Senate Minority Leader Mark Johnson spoke at a press conference shortly after the legislative session ended on May 20, 2024. The GOP leaders denounced the 1,400 page omnibus bill, which they displayed on the podium and was passed by the Democratic majority in the closing moments of the 2024 legislative session. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer.)A conservative legal organization is representing homebuilders in a lawsuit aimed at invalidating parts of — if not all of — a 1,400 page mega-bill passed by the DFL-controlled Legislature in the chaotic final minutes of the 2024 legislative session. 
The Minnesota Constitution requires that bills address a single subject, and that the title of the bill reflects that subject. Democratic-Farmer-Labor lawmakers assembled and passed the omnibus in the final shambolic hours of the 2024 legislative session following days of filibustering by Republican lawmakers, who shouted “Shame!” and “Follow the rules!” on the House floor as the DFL voted on the bill. 
The bill contained a wide range of new laws, from minimum pay rates for Uber and Lyft drivers to increased penalties for straw gun purchases and changes to the state’s paid leave law. The bill’s title was more than five pages long.
Previous plaintiffs suing over the same issue have already succeeded in getting parts of the bill overturned, and the continued litigation is a cautionary tale for future legislatures that try to cram all their bills into a mega-bill. Although the 2024 example is the most extreme in memory, legislative majorities of both parties have often loaded bills into mega-bills out of legislative and political expediency. 
Central Minnesota Builders Association and Rochester Area Builders Inc. are the plaintiffs in the lawsuit filed Monday by attorneys with the Upper Midwest Law Center. The lawsuit challenges the construction industry regulations in the bill, including restrictions on the use of independent contractors; new registration rules for construction companies; and, a requirement that the state residential energy code reduce net energy consumption by 70% by 2038.
The lawsuit asks that a state judge invalidate the entirety of the 2024 bill under the Constitution’s single subject clause — or to at least strike down its construction-related laws.
“This mega-omnibus bill creates an earthquake of increased costs and opportunities for fraud in our state,” said Nicholas Nelson, an attorney with the Upper Midwest Law Center. 
The Upper Midwest Law Center, representing the Minnesota Gun Owners Caucus, already successfully overturned one major policy provision in the bill: a ban on binary triggers, which increase the rate of fire of semiautomatic firearms. 
In that case, Ramsey County District Judge Leonardo Castro wrote that “the 2024 Omnibus Bill violates the Single Subject and Title Clause, because, at best, it contains many non-germane parts, and at worst, has no identifiable common theme.”
The ruling set the stage for further lawsuits from conservative organizations challenging other portions of the bill. Nelson said Monday’s lawsuit is the fifth such case.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma’s GOP Legislature left out key info on property taxes state question: the financial impact
text:
The downtown Oklahoma City skyline is pictured. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)If any emoji best represents the property tax state question Oklahoma lawmakers have placed before voters, it would be the grimace.
For those who need a translation, we use that face to express tension. In this case, it’s because our Republican-controlled Legislature, in all its wisdom, tacked on this disclaimer to their proposed constitutional amendment: “If passed, this measure would have a fiscal impact on the state, but the exact impact is unknown.”
(Insert eye-roll emoji.)
Lawmakers, in their zest to convince us they are cutting taxes as inflation rages on, decided that taking the time to suss out how eliminating a chunk of revenue via State Question 847 will affect senior citizens, public schools, CareerTechs, counties and some municipalities wasn’t as important as having a talking point on the campaign trail.
Because that’s where our property taxes go. Reminder: property taxes typically fund the functions of municipal and county governments. State government doesn’t get a dime from these taxes.  
Maybe that’s why they weren’t sure about the fiscal impact?
I don’t know whether this oversight was sheer laziness, a blatant disregard for voter intelligence or if legislators’ effort was a rush job that overlooked the finer details – including how complicated it probably is to calculate the impact.
But in any case, this is an unfair scenario for Oklahoma voters who have to make a decision on Nov. 3 about whether to change the structure of our property tax system. Voters deserve to have all the facts ahead of time, and lawmakers should not be permitted to omit them.
Since they did, though, I’ll fill in the gaps.
An Oklahoma Tax Commission analysis estimates local jurisdictions would lose about $45.78 million in revenue in the first year if voters approve this question. Over the next 10 years, that lost revenue could top $450 million.
That’s a whopping sum of money for a ballot measure that lists its fiscal impact as being “unknown.”
State Question 847 is one of the most convoluted and complicated state questions on the ballot this year, and that’s saying a lot given some of the other issues that lawmakers have placed before voters. (Who can forget that manufacturing tax credit that voters soundly rejected in August?)
Right now, the fair cash value of a home can’t increase by more than 3% a year for homesteads — better known as the homes we own and live in — and for most agricultural land. Commercial property values are capped at no more than a 5% annual increase.
Lawmakers have decided it’s time to lower that cap to a seemingly random 1.75% a year for homesteads and agricultural properties and to 4% for commercial properties. 
They also have decided to muck around with the income cap that senior citizens must meet to qualify for a valuation freeze. The amount of the increase would be calculated on a tiered system ranging from 0% to 1.75% based on a formula that is way too complicated.
Supporters argue that the measure would create the “lowest cap on growth” for homesteads in the U.S. and save cash-strapped Oklahomans money.
Critics, though, point out that besides the previously mentioned budget cuts for public schools, CareerTechs, county governments and some municipalities, it would also make it harder for those entities to borrow money for future needs.
They say this is not really property tax relief. The value of properties will continue to go up, and so will Oklahoman’s taxes. This merely just slows the rate of growth a bit.
But they also warn that because it will reduce revenue, many Oklahomans should expect to see their tax rates go up to pay the existing bills.
That’s because bond debt – that borrowed money I just mentioned – will not miraculously vanish. All bonds are set based on the revenue expected to be generated from existing property taxes. When someone screws around with the formula, it messes up those expected revenue streams.
The only feasible way right now to make up that lost revenue is to adjust the millage rates — better known as the tax rate assessed on real estate. That means everyone will see an increase in their taxes, but I suspect senior citizens living on fixed incomes could feel the pinch more.
Lower-income senior citizens’ home valuations have long been frozen to provide them an idea of what their tax bills will look like each year. Most probably have not budgeted to abruptly pay higher taxes.
How much millage rates will increase depends on how reliant an entity is on the revenue source and whether local jurisdictions have enough resources to adjust. 
Rural residents in particular will likely be harder hit because those entities have less resources to draw on. 
So instead of cutting expenses at the state government level that they control, lawmakers plan to force those cuts on local governments. How is that fair?
Oklahomans’ wallets definitely need relief from soaring property insurance and utility rates as well as high gas, diesel and grocery prices, but this plan doesn’t do anything to address that.
Maybe rather than monkeying around with our property tax formulas, lawmakers should first look at why their policies have resulted in us having the highest homeowners insurance rates in the country — more than double the national average. Reducing those rates would certainly provide welcome relief without harming our local revenue streams.
But it seems like state leaders prefer to live in a fairy tale where instead of apples or peaches, money grows on trees for the benefit of our cities and towns. And instead of doing the hard work of confronting insurance lobbyists and fixing broken state spending, it’s easier to ask voters to pass a plan with an unknown budgetary impact.
Here’s the reality: No business wants to come to a community that doesn’t have good schools, good roads and bridges and solid public services. Those services are primarily paid for by property taxes. 
To put this plan back in emoji speak: big red question mark.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT can opt to help students through a new federal tax program
text:
It seems everyone is talking about Nicole Hannah-Jones’ recent New York Times piece describing the educational experiences of her daughter, Najya, in the New York City public schools. If you haven’t read it, suffice to say that those experiences were less than ideal.
In recent days there have been dozens, if not hundreds, of commentaries on Hannah-Jones’ piece, and each one seems to have a different take on who is the villain in the story. Writing in the NY Post, Daniel di Martino insists that it is teacher’s unions. In the Free Press, Coleman Hughes suggests that an unwillingness to discipline disruptive children is a large part of the problem. In Slate, Jill Filipovic identifies no clear villain, but notes we need to make sure we are, ”not lowering the bar just because some students have a harder time clearing it.”
What all the commentators can agree on is that many, many schools in the United States are deeply dysfunctional. And, for this reason, many, many U.S. school children are receiving (as Hughes puts it in the Free Press), “[not just] a subpar education; they get no education, period.”
Fortunately, help is on the way. In 2025 the federal government created a provision that could put over $270 billion dollars every year into our educational system. The money would come from an optional tax credit (the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit) which, starting January 1, allows each U.S. citizen who owes at least $1,700 in taxes to (instead of paying tax) donate up to that amount to a scholarship granting organization (SGO) of his or her choice. Unlike a tax deduction, the credit means the donation is completely cost-free to the taxpayer.
The SGOs would take the money raised and use it to pay for educational expenses for children in their respective states.  The term SGO is a misnomer, since the money disbursed need not be a scholarship in a traditional sense.  It could be used for any “qualified elementary or secondary education expense” and could be given to both public and private school students.  The law specifically allows expenses as diverse as books, technology, tutoring, extended day programs and special needs services.
Hannah-Jones’ article points out that disadvantaged school districts typically have less money available to them even though their student bodies have higher needs.  This is primarily because public schools in the U.S. are mostly funded from local property tax receipts. Raising taxes is clearly not possible in poorer areas where citizens are already struggling to make ends meet. The new tax credit breaks down the correlation between local property tax revenues and resources available to schools, providing a new mechanism for monies to flow to under-resourced schools.
What is the catch, you ask? Only one. Any taxpayer is eligible to donate (again, at no cost to him or herself) to a qualified SGO. However, if you want your gift to go to help students in your state, your governor has to opt in to the program. If not, you can only donate to a scholarship granting organization in a state whose governor has opted in.
You would think it would be a no-brainer for states to opt-in. However, the IRS reports that as of October 13, 31 have done so and Connecticut is not one of them.  SGOs need time to plan to handle the new donations that will be coming in. 
Given the potential benefit to their neediest students, my only question is, “What is Connecticut waiting for?”
Christopher Rhoads is an associate professor in the Neag School of Education at the University of Connecticut.  The views expressed here are his own and do not represent those of his institution.

name: VTDigger
title: To tax or not to tax: Two towns consider a local option tax this November
text:
Hinesburg Town Hall seen in November 2021. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Stowe’s highway foreman was driving this summer when he came upon an unpleasant sight: a hole in the deck of the Weeks Hill Road bridge.
Many Vermont towns would need to wait a long time to access state funding for bridge repairs, Will Fricke, Stowe’s assistant city manager, said.
But Stowe had a revenue source tucked away.
“Because of local option taxes, we were lucky enough to, you know, have those capital reserves in order to fix that bridge ourselves,” said Fricke, who is hoping to have the bridge construction completed by Thanksgiving.
In the past 20 years, local option taxes have become increasingly popular in municipalities across Vermont. These taxes can be adopted in three different ways. Municipalities can choose to add a 1% tax on top of the 6% state sales tax, the 9% state meals and rooms tax and the 10% state alcoholic beverage tax. The meals and alcoholic beverages tax must be applied together, according to the Vermont government website.
The tax increase proposals come with no shortage of controversy.
The taxes are touted by many city officials as a way to generate revenue, stabilize property taxes and balance out tourists’ impacts on infrastructure and services. Opponents worry about the effects on local businesses and residents and wonder if the proposals will be as effective in towns with smaller tourist presences. This November, Hinesburg and Bennington will both vote on a local option tax for sales, rooms and meals and alcohol in their communities.
The price to sustain a city is only getting higher, said Joy Dubin Grossman, Hinesburg’s assistant town manager. These taxes are an “additional lever” that the town can use to fund necessary services and projects, she said, so it will have less need to increase property taxes.
In Hinesburg, the town estimates that the local option tax could generate between $275,000 and $330,000 in revenue annually. The town would use the revenue for public safety, infrastructure and decreasing reliance on property taxes.
Hinesburg’s local option tax was a topic of discussion in a recent town meeting, according to the Hinesburg Record. Aaron Miller, a meeting attendee, said in an interview that he could see the benefits. Still, he said he would like more clarification on the amount of tax revenue coming from visitors as opposed to community members.
“I mean, obviously, Hinesburg is not Stowe, and so our ability to raise that sales tax or meals and rooms in significant amounts is much lower,” Miller said.
In Bennington, the local option tax would apply to sales, meals and alcoholic beverages and rooms, according to their proposed policy. The selectboard estimates that the tax will bring in about $1.8 million in additional revenue. The proposal requires at least 50% of annual revenue to go toward stabilizing the local property tax rate, increasing to 89% in fiscal year 2027-2028.
The idea has been controversial in Bennington, according to Jonah Spivak, the town’s communications coordinator.
A preliminary poll conducted in Bennington showed support for the local option tax, Spivak said, with 40% of people indicating they would vote yes and 18% of people saying they would likely vote yes. But around 90% of the respondents were property owners in the community, which means they’d experience more direct property tax relief, he said.
“People are asking, ‘Well, what’s in it for those who are not property taxpayers?’” Spivak said. 
But Gordon Black, Manchester’s town assessor and economic development officer, has lived and worked in both Bennington and Manchester and seen the impacts of Manchester’s local option tax since its implementation.
From July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, Manchester’s local option tax generated $1,737,618 for the town, according to the Manchester Journal. The town was able to decrease overall property taxes for fiscal year 2026.
Black said the tax can be especially impactful in communities with significant tourist traffic such as Manchester, but there could also be powerful impacts in Bennington due to its large department and grocery stores.
“If you go to the Walmart, or you go to any of the grocery stores or Home Depot, there are a lot of New York cars and frequently Massachusetts cars there,” Black said. “So people come from everywhere to go to those larger stores.”
Black added that the perception that renters would not benefit is largely skewed, since higher property tax rates for landlords translate into higher rents.
“They’re paying for that higher property tax, no question about it,” Black said.
In Stowe, Fricke said the local option tax has helped the town repair infrastructure. If it embarks on a large project, Fricke said Stowe can utilize that revenue instead of taxes spiking for a year.
The biggest project that Stowe has been able to accomplish is a large-scale improvement of the sidewalks on its main street, and a project that placed the street’s power lines underground.
Wilmington’s selectboard took a different approach to infrastructure repair this year, awarding $50,000 to businesses in their town center who took revenue hits this summer due to road construction, according to the Deerfield Valley News. Businesses might also need extra help in 2029, when a planned bridge replacement will close Route 9.
Stowe passed a local option sales tax in addition to its meals and rooms tax in 2023, which Fricke said is directed to the general fund to alleviate property taxes.
Montpelier has seen positive results since the implementation of a local option tax in 2025, according to Finance Director Heather Graves. In fiscal year 2027, it will be used to provide tax relief to Montpelier’s residents, she said, and it has helped the city purchase essential equipment like a new ambulance.
Miller, the Hinesburg resident who spoke at a recent meeting, said data about visitor spending versus resident spending would make this an easier decision for Hinesburg, but the absence of that information complicates things.
“I think Hinesburg will ultimately end up needing to make an imperfect decision,” Miller said.
